decisions.reason: The spec said only that a note is named from its title. It now fixes a normalisation rule, refuses unsafe or empty titles, never overwrites, and requires no-follow opens.
Update-before-create had no testable rule for the helper. save now takes an explicit into target, refuses when the text overlaps a note by word count, and records a new-despite choice.
The path from the owner answer to keep was missing. The spec now has drop and merge commands, a second review for a new digest, and a digest that covers the exact set keep moves.
Expiry had no trigger or visibility. It now runs lazily at the start of save, list, wings and review, is idempotent, and archived notes are hidden unless asked for.
list and read had no way to name an archived note. Both now take a state option with reviewed, draft, archived and all, with a stated default and a refusal for an ambiguous name.
Atomicity covered one save only. Merge, drop and keep now have an ordered write sequence, a journal for keep, retry rules, and tests that stop each operation after every step.

The credential scan was not testable. The spec now lists a minimum set of patterns, scans the complete note including the result of an into save, reports the line number and pattern name only, and has no override.

Real conflict: at most one ask against two confirmed commands. The spec now defines one review exchange: the summary, one owner reply, and the harness confirmations of the keep command and the filing command.
Review and keep had no wing selector. Both now work on one wing, keep requires a wing, and the journal, lock and digest are per wing.
The collision check skipped the archive, so reuse of a name could replace an archived note. The check now includes the archive, and archiving adds a UTC time suffix so no entry is ever replaced.

Drop and merge could not name a wing or tell a title from a file name. The spec now has one note syntax, limits drop and merge to drafts, keeps merge inside one wing, and refuses a self-merge and unsafe names.
The new option was said to cope with equal normalised names, which it could not. A name collision is now always a refusal and the agent picks another title; the option only allows overlapping text.
